details:
**Cinnabar**
The main ore of the element mercury, made of mercury(II) sulfide (HgS). When ground, it gives the bright red pigment vermilion, and roasting it releases mercury metal.

**Amalgams**
The name for alloys of mercury with other metals. Silver-tin amalgams have long been used as dental fillings for cavities, and mercury was once used to extract silver from ore by amalgamation in the patio process.

**Millimeters of mercury (mmHg) and the torr**
Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature, so it was used in the first barometers. Standard atmospheric pressure holds up a column of mercury 760 mm tall, and one torr is about one millimeter of mercury. Daniel Fahrenheit also used mercury in his thermometers.

**Methylmercury and Minamata disease**
Methylmercury is an organic mercury compound that bioaccumulates and biomagnifies up food chains, reaching high levels in large predatory fish such as tuna and shark. Industrial mercury dumped into Minamata Bay in Japan caused mass poisoning known as Minamata disease, and pregnant women are advised to limit eating such fish.

**MESSENGER probe**
The NASA spacecraft that orbited the planet Mercury from 2011 until it crashed into the surface in 2015. Its findings included evidence for water ice in permanently shadowed polar craters. Mariner 10 was the earlier flyby probe, and the joint ESA-JAXA mission BepiColombo is the next one.

**Caloris Basin and the "weird terrain"**
The Caloris Basin is one of the largest impact craters in the solar system, and it contains the spider-shaped Pantheon Fossae trough system around Apollodorus crater. Directly opposite it on the planet lies a hilly, jumbled region called the "weird terrain," thought to have formed when shock waves from the Caloris impact converged there.

**3:2 spin-orbit resonance**
The planet Mercury rotates exactly three times for every two orbits around the Sun. It was once thought to be tidally locked. Because of this resonance, one solar day lasts two Mercury years, and at certain points the Sun briefly appears to reverse direction in the sky.

**Calomel electrode**
A common reference electrode that uses mercury in contact with calomel, which is mercury(I) chloride (Hg₂Cl₂). The saturated calomel electrode uses saturated potassium chloride. Calomel contains the Hg₂²⁺ ion, an example of mercury's tendency to form polycations.

**Precession of the perihelion and general relativity**
Mercury's orbit precesses slightly more than Newtonian gravity predicts. Urbain Le Verrier proposed an unseen inner planet, Vulcan, to explain this, but Einstein's general relativity accounted for the extra precession exactly. This was one of the first confirmations of the theory.

**Castner-Kellner process**
A version of the chloralkali process that electrolyzes brine over a layer of liquid mercury at the bottom of the cell. The mercury acts as the cathode and forms a sodium amalgam, which then reacts with water to give sodium hydroxide, while chlorine gas forms at the anode.

**Oxymercuration-demercuration and the Clemmensen reduction**
In oxymercuration-demercuration, mercury(II) acetate and water add across an alkene, and sodium borohydride then removes the mercury. This gives the Markovnikov alcohol without carbocation rearrangements. In the Clemmensen reduction, zinc amalgam and hydrochloric acid reduce aldehydes and ketones to alkanes.

**Thimerosal (thiomersal)**
An organomercury compound in which mercury is bonded to sulfur, once widely used as a preservative in vaccines. Concern over its mercury content led to its removal or ban in many vaccines. Thiols are also called "mercaptans," meaning "mercury capturing," because of their strong affinity for mercury.

**Dimethylmercury and Karen Wetterhahn**
Dimethylmercury is an extremely toxic compound once used as an NMR reference standard. Dartmouth chemist Karen Wetterhahn died in 1997 after a few drops seeped through her latex gloves.

**Nessler's reagent**
A solution of potassium tetraiodomercurate(II) (K₂[HgI₄]) in base, in which mercury is bound to four iodine atoms. It turns yellow to brown in the presence of ammonia and is used to detect small amounts of it.

**Smallest planet with a huge iron core**
Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun, with no moons, the most eccentric orbit, the smallest axial tilt, and only a thin exosphere instead of an atmosphere. Its iron core makes up most of its radius, which may be explained by a giant impact stripping off its outer layers.
